summary: Root cause (confidence 0.62, medium): portfolio-service v4.5.0 (dep-5905, deployed 08:56Z) added an unindexed query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at with no accompanying migration; that query drives sequential scans of a ~48M-row trades table on the shared ledger-db, pinning the DB host at ~96% CPU, tripling connections and lifting slow queries from ~1/min to ~140/min, which in turn causes order-service's INSERT INTO orders to exceed its statement timeout (p99 ~5s, error rate ~9%). The alternative hypotheses are actively contradicted rather than merely unproven: the 08:00Z autovacuum config change (cfg-2903) showed zero effect for 55 minutes and no vacuum log lines in the onset window, order-service's own CPU/memory/request-rate are flat with only DB statement-timeout errors, and disk_used_pct and replication_lag_ms are flat across onset, ruling out IOPS throttling/disk pressure. Confidence is capped because the micro-mechanism (unindexed, high-volume, live request path) is supported by a logged seq-scan slow query plus the HIST-111 precedent rather than by index/EXPLAIN/pg_stat evidence, which no available tool can provide.

ranked_hypotheses.title: portfolio-service v4.5.0 unindexed query on trades drives ledger-db CPU/connection saturation
ranked_hypotheses.statement: dep-5905 (portfolio-service v4.5.0, deployed 08:56Z) added a query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at with no migration/index. That query causes sequential scans of a very large trades table on the shared ledger-db, pinning the DB host at ~96% CPU and lifting slow_queries from ~1/min to ~140/min with connections tripling. order-service's own INSERT INTO orders then exceeds its statement timeout (p99 ~5s, error rate ~9%). The decisive new evidence is log-level: the first ledger-db WARN in the onset window is portfolioservice's own seq-scan slow query (8690ms, 'Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)', application_name=portfolio-service) at 08:58:38Z — three minutes after the metric step and the same bucket as the deploy — and it repeats.

causal_chain.claim: portfolio-service v4.5.0 deploys at 08:56Z with a new trades query on (account_id, executed_at) and explicitly no migration/index
The new query runs on ledger-db as a Seq Scan over trades (rows=48.2M), logging 8.69s slow queries from 08:58:38Z in portfolio-service's application_name
ledger-db CPU steps from ~29-31% to ~74-96% in the 08:57 bucket and pins at ~95-96% through 10:24Z; slow_queries 0.7-1.2/min -> ~93-148/min; connections 59-65 -> ~148-200 in the same bucket
The saturated DB slows all queries on ledger-db, so order-service's INSERT INTO orders exceeds the statement timeout
order-service db_pool_in_use climbs to its ceiling (~44-51) as slow statements hold connections, and p99 reaches ~5.0-5.6s
portfolio-service, the deployer, shows the worst latency (~7s) in the identical 08:58 onset bucket

assumptions: The 48.2M-row seq scan observed at 08:58:38Z is the query introduced by v4.5.0 (the log ties it to portfolio-service but not explicitly to the deploy).
The query is executed at meaningful volume repeatedly, not once — F29 shows four occurrences in ~70s, which supports but does not fully confirm sustained load.
No supporting index on (account_id, executed_at) exists; F29's 'Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)' is strong evidence for this but is a log snapshot, not an index listing.
payment-service and settlement-service stay healthy because their queries hit indexed columns or their own tables on ledger-db.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Ledger-db host capacity saturation (CPU) from aggregate load, no single triggering change
ranked_hypotheses.statement: ledger-db had grown to the edge of its provisioned CPU capacity and naturally tipped into ~96% saturation, throttling all queries including order-service INSERTs.

causal_chain.claim: Sustained aggregate query load across the four db-edge consumers pushes the host to ~96% CPU
CPU saturation slows all queries; connections accumulate as queries linger
order-service INSERTs exceed statement timeout and p99 reaches ~5s

assumptions: Demand on ledger-db stepped sharply at 08:55Z for a non-change reason.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Capacity saturation from gradual demand growth requires a smooth rise, but every ledger-db metric is dead flat for hours and then steps within a single 3-min bucket: CPU 29-31% in all buckets 08:00-08:54Z then 74-96% at 08:57Z; slow_queries 0.7-1.2/min then 93-148/min; connections 59-65 then 148-200 (F25, F26, F27, F30). order-service request_rate is likewise flat at ~231 req/s with no growth (F15). A step, not a ramp, plus a deploy at 08:56Z points to a new workload rather than accumulated volume.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Ledger-db volume IOPS throttling / burst-credit exhaustion (repeat of HIST-110)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The cloud volume backing ledger-db exhausted burst credits or hit an IOPS throttle, stalling I/O so queries slowed and statement timeouts followed, matching HIST-110.

causal_chain.claim: ledger-db volume burst credits exhausted / IOPS throttled (HIST-110 precedent)
I/O stall slows queries, raising slow_queries and stacking connections
order-service INSERTs exceed statement timeout; p99 climbs to ~5s

assumptions: Unobservable IOPS behavior would show throttling that leaves CPU-pinned and flat-disk/lag fingerprints.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: This is now squarely contradicted. disk_used_pct is flat at 70.6-71.8% across the whole window, including fine 4-min buckets around onset with no step (F31, F32), and replication_lag_ms is flat at ~40ms across 07:00-10:59Z with no degradation at onset (F33) — an I/O stall would disturb both. The observed pattern is CPU pinned at ~96% (F4, F16), and ledger-db does expose no IOPS metric at all (F34), so there is no positive evidence of throttling. HIST-110 is a keyword-scored lead, not evidence (F23). The timestamped seq-scan log from portfolio-service at 08:58:38Z gives a concrete competing mechanism (F29).

ranked_hypotheses.title: DBA autovacuum scale-factor change causes heavy vacuum IO/CPU and lock contention on ledger-db
ranked_hypotheses.statement: cfg-2903 changed autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1 at 08:00Z, and the resulting vacuum maintenance load slowed ledger-db enough that order-service INSERTs timed out. The reporter's suspicion.

causal_chain.claim: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor lowered to 0.1 at 08:00Z makes autovacuum more aggressive on ledger-db
Aggressive vacuum consumes CPU/IO and adds lock contention on ledger-db tables
ledger-db CPU pins at ~96%, slow_queries jump to ~140/min, connections triple

assumptions: A heavy vacuum phase would have to arrive ~55 minutes after the threshold change without any earlier metric effect.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Timing and log evidence rule this out. ledger-db CPU, slow_queries and connections are flat at baseline in every 3-min bucket from 08:00 through 08:54Z — 55 minutes with zero measurable effect from the 08:00:20Z config change (F25, F26, F27, F30). The autovacuum activity that did run logged routine 'processed table public.audit_log' INFO lines ending at 08:52:26Z, ~3 min BEFORE the 08:55 metric step, and a contains='vacuum' log query over 08:55-09:20Z returns 0 matches (F28, F29). The step at 08:55-08:57 coincides with the 08:56Z portfolio-service deploy, and the first WARN is a portfolio-service seq-scan slow query, not any vacuum event (F29). Lowering the scale factor also makes vacuum more aggressive, which would not by itself pin CPU at 96% with no vacuum log activity.

ranked_hypotheses.title: order-service application-side degradation (pool exhaustion / retry amplification) originating in the app
ranked_hypotheses.statement: order-service's own datasource pool ceiling or retry behaviour caused its queries to queue and time out, with ledger-db load a consequence rather than a cause.

causal_chain.claim: order-service db pool reaches its ceiling (44-47 of ~51 in use)
Requests queue behind the pool ceiling and retries multiply concurrent DB queries
Amplified load drives ledger-db CPU to ~96% and slow_queries to ~140/min

assumptions: order-service's pool is misconfigured pre-existing despite no change this week.
Retry amplification occurs without any request-rate growth.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: order-service CPU (flat 35.6-44.4%), memory (59.6-60.8%) and request_rate (~231 req/s) all show no step at onset (F14, F15); its p99 was stable at ~150ms for hours. All its errors are DB statement timeouts on INSERT INTO orders with no connection-refused/pool-wait/GC signature (F13). portfolio-service — a different ledger-db consumer — degrades at the same instant to an even worse ~7s while running a newly deployed seq-scan query (F17, F29). An order-service-originated fault cannot explain portfolio-service's simultaneous collapse nor payment-service/settlement-service stability (F18, F35).

facts.statement: order-service p99 latency was flat at ~145-165ms from 06:00 through 08:56Z, then jumped in the 08:56-08:58Z bucket (avg 2878ms, max 5607.8ms) and stayed ~5000-5600ms through 10:54Z.
order-service error_rate rose from ~0.2% baseline to ~9.3-9.6% in the same 08:55Z onset bucket as the latency jump.
ledger-db slow_queries_per_min rose from ~1/min baseline to 82.59 (max 148.81) in the 08:55Z bucket and stayed ~135-143/min through 10:54Z.
ledger-db cpu_pct jumped from steady ~29-31% to 67.67% (max 96.36) in the 08:55Z bucket and pinned at ~95-97% through 10:54Z.
ledger-db connections_active rose from ~61-63 baseline to 134.52 (max 199.81) in the 08:55Z bucket and held ~189-199 (max 212.35) through 10:54Z.
order-service db_pool_in_use rose from ~13.8-14.5 to 27.9 (max 47.97) in the same onset bucket, holding ~44-47 (max 51.63) — saturated near ceiling.

The only deployment in the entire window (2026-05-04 00:00Z - 2026-05-05 10:59Z) is dep-5905, portfolio-service v4.5.0, deployed 2026-05-05T08:56:00Z, with 'new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at' and 'no migration included'; status live, never rolled back. No order-service deployment appears.

The only config change in the window is cfg-2903 on ledger-db: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1 at 2026-05-05T08:00:00Z by dba-team; no schema/index/migration change is listed anywhere and ledger-db had zero deployments.
order-service depends directly on ledger-db, which is flagged shared=true and has db edges from four services: order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service.

All 51 order-service WARN/ERROR log entries between 08:40Z and 09:20Z are a single signature: 'ledger-db: canceling statement due to statement timeout (INSERT INTO orders)', first at 09:00:42Z, continuing every ~1-2 min; no connection-refused, pool-wait, or GC-pause signatures.

order-service CPU is flat and not saturated across the event (avg 39.7-40.5% per 7-min bucket 08:30-10:57Z, max 44.4%), and memory (~59.6-60.8%) and request_rate (~231 req/s) are likewise flat with no step at onset.
portfolio-service latency jumped in the same 08:58Z bucket from ~177-183ms baseline to 6985ms avg (max 7212.58) and held ~6.7-7.2s through 10:57Z.

payment-service latency stays flat ~310-326ms and settlement-service is completely unaffected (latency mean 240.28ms, error_rate ~0.22%, db_pool_in_use mean 6.02) across the window, so the symptom is not uniformly hitting all ledger-db consumers.

ledger-db cpu_pct, slow_queries_per_min and connections_active are all dead flat at baseline in every 3-min bucket from 08:00Z through 08:54Z, then step only in the 08:57Z bucket (08:55-08:58) — the 08:00:20Z autovacuum change produced no measurable effect for ~55 minutes.

ledger-db logs 08:00-09:00Z contain only 7 routine INFO 'autovacuum: processed table public.audit_log' lines, the last at 08:52:26Z (~3 min before the metric step), with no worker launch/finish, duration, bloat or lock-wait entries; a contains='vacuum' log query over 08:55-09:20Z returns 0 matches.

The first WARN in the 08:00-09:00Z ledger-db log window is a seq-scan slow query from portfolio-service at 08:58:38Z ('slow query 8690ms: SELECT * FROM trades WHERE account_id=$1 AND executed_at > $2 ... Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907) application_name=portfolio-service'), repeating three more times within ~70s (08:58:50Z, 08:59:37Z, 08:59:48Z).

ledger-db disk_used_pct is flat at ~70.6-71.8% across the whole 07:00-10:59Z window with no step at onset even at 4-minute granularity, and replication_lag_ms is flat at ~40ms across 07:00-10:59Z with no degradation at onset.

The ledger-db metric source exposes no IOPS, throughput, queue-depth or volume-throttle indicator (available metrics: connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min).

No tool in the available surface can introspect ledger-db schema or SQL statistics: indexes on trades, EXPLAIN/query plans, trades row count/size, and pg_stat_statements/pg_stat_activity call counts and blocked sessions for 08:00-10:59Z are all unavailable.

Historical precedent HIST-111 (ledger-db + settlement-service) attributes a matching incident to 'New report query without index did sequential scans' (category bad_deployment, symptoms slow queries / high db cpu, resolution 'Added index; query review gate'); HIST-110 (IOPS throttling) remains a live keyword-scored precedent, so symptom vocabulary alone does not separate the mechanisms.

assumptions: The 48.2M-row seq scan logged at 08:58:38Z is the query introduced by portfolio-service v4.5.0 — the log ties it to portfolio-service (application_name) but not explicitly to the deploy.

The v4.5.0 query is executed at meaningful volume repeatedly on the live request path; four occurrences in ~70s (F29) is consistent with sustained load but is a log snapshot, not a call-count measurement.
No index supporting (account_id, executed_at) exists on trades; the logged 'Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)' is strong evidence but is not an index listing.
payment-service and settlement-service stay healthy because their queries hit indexed columns or other tables on ledger-db, i.e. differing access paths rather than a non-existent shared cause.

The order-service statement timeouts are a consequence of ledger-db CPU/connection saturation and not an independent order-service-side fault; supported by flat app-side CPU/memory/request_rate plus the identical-timing portfolio-service collapse.

The 08:56Z deploy is causally linked to the 08:55-08:58Z metric step; the 3-minute metric bucket cannot fully separate the deploy from other same-bucket events, though the 08:00Z config change is excluded by 55 minutes of flat baseline.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Change timeline relative to the 09:10Z report: autovacuum config 08:00Z -> portfolio-service deploy 08:56Z -> report 09:10Z; neither change has been rolled back.

All three ledger-db metrics step in the 08:57 bucket (CPU avg 74.71, slow_queries avg 93.39, connections avg 148.34), reaching 94.07% / 148.81 / 191.88 by 09:00Z.

First ledger-db WARN of the window: portfolio-service seq-scan slow query, 8690ms, 'Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)', application_name=portfolio-service; repeats at 08:58:50Z, 08:59:37Z and 08:59:48Z.

recommended_actions.action: Roll back dep-5905 (portfolio-service v4.5.0, deployed 2026-05-05T08:56:00Z) to the previous portfolio-service release immediately, or if rollback is not possible, disable/feature-flag off the 'realised P&L breakdown' holdings API path that issues the new trades query, to remove the seq-scan load from ledger-db.
recommended_actions.rationale: H1's mechanism is the only one with a logged, concrete tie to the shared DB: the first ledger-db WARN at onset is portfolio-service's own 8690ms seq scan of 48.2M rows, and portfolio-service has the worst latency (~7s) while the deploy is the sole change near the 08:55-08:58 step. Removing the new workload is the safe, targeted mitigation.

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT revert cfg-2903 (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1) as a first-line mitigation, and do not treat the DBA change as the cause; if rollback is attempted, record it explicitly as a test rather than a fix.
recommended_actions.rationale: The 08:00Z config change had ~55 minutes with zero measurable effect (ledger-db CPU/slow_queries/connections flat through 08:54Z), its last log line is 08:52:26Z and there are zero 'vacuum' log matches in 08:55-09:20Z — reverting it would add change risk without addressing the observed step.

recommended_actions.action: After the rollback, verify recovery on the same signals that defined onset: ledger-db cpu_pct should fall from ~95-97% back toward ~29-31%, slow_queries_per_min from ~140/min back toward ~1/min, connections_active from ~190-200 back toward ~60, and order-service p99 from ~5-5.6s back to ~150ms with error_rate back to ~0.2%.
recommended_actions.rationale: These are the exact verified metrics whose simultaneous step at 08:55-08:58Z defines the incident; recovery of all five is the discriminator that confirms the new trades query was the load source rather than a coincidental co-mover.

recommended_actions.action: Ship a migration adding a supporting index on trades (account_id, executed_at) before re-enabling the v4.5.0 query path, and add the same query-review gate HIST-111's resolution calls for before deploys that touch large shared tables.
recommended_actions.rationale: The deploy annotation explicitly says 'no migration included' while the observed plan is 'Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)'; HIST-111 resolved an identical seq-scan-on-ledger-db incident with 'Added index; query review gate'.

recommended_actions.action: Add guardrails so a single consumer's heavy query on shared ledger-db cannot pin the host: per-service statement timeout and work_mem/connection limits or resource governance on ledger-db, plus alerting on ledger-db cpu_pct > 80%, slow_queries_per_min > 20, and connections_active > 100.
recommended_actions.rationale: ledger-db is shared=true across four services and one service's unindexed query tripled connections and pinned CPU at 96% (F4, F5); the blast radius is structural, and slow_queries_per_min rose from ~1/min to ~140/min before anyone acted.

recommended_actions.action: Make unindexed-access detection routine: alert on new query shapes against large tables (pg_stat_statements seq-scan/rows-scanned thresholds) and require index coverage review as part of deployment review for services with db edges to shared datastores.
recommended_actions.rationale: The failure mode was a new query on a very large table shipped with no migration and no plan review (F21, F29); HIST-111 and HIST-115 show this class of incident has recurred in the same estate.

recommended_actions.action: If rollback does not restore the metrics, capture the discriminating evidence that is currently missing: pg_stat_statements call counts and pg_stat_activity blocked sessions for 08:00-10:59Z, EXPLAIN of the v4.5.0 trades query, and index inventory on trades.
recommended_actions.rationale: These are the four unanswered questions (F19) that would convert the H1 micro-mechanism from strongly indicated to proven, and they are also the fastest way to separate H1 from H5 if mitigation fails.

data_gaps: No tool exposes ledger-db schema, index definitions (pg_indexes), EXPLAIN/query plans, trades table row count/size, or pg_stat_statements/pg_stat_activity — so 'unindexed + high-volume + on the live request path' rests on the 08:58:38Z seq-scan log line plus the HIST-111 precedent, not on direct schema/plan/call-count evidence (F19). This is the main reason confidence is capped at medium.

ledger-db exposes no IOPS, throughput, queue-depth or volume-throttle metric and no lock-wait metric (available: connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min), and query_latency_ms is permanently unavailable, so H5 IOPS throttling is excluded by absence of disk/lag pressure rather than by a positive signal (F34).

ledger-db log source is application-level only (config, checkpoint, autovacuum summary, slow query) — no autovacuum worker launch/finish, vacuum duration, dead-tuple/bloat or lock-wait detail, so a short vacuum-induced lock/IO spike cannot be positively excluded from logs alone (F28, F29).

order-service exposes no GC, thread-pool or queue-depth metric (only cpu_pct, db_pool_in_use, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts), so GC pauses or internal pool queueing cannot be excluded beyond the flat CPU/memory/request-rate evidence (F15).

order-service logs before 09:00Z could not be checked (the 08:40-09:00Z WARN+ window returned 0 matches and the final log query hit budget_exhausted), so whether any app-side pool-wait or retry signature preceded the first DB statement timeout at 09:00:42Z is unresolved.
settlement-service WARN/ERROR logs were never queried (tool budget exhausted), so its healthy state rests on flat latency/error/pool metrics alone (F35).
The exact onset time is pinned only to the 3-minute 08:55-08:58Z bucket, so the 08:56Z deploy cannot be separated from other same-bucket events by timing alone (F30).
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Discovery of an existing index on trades(account_id, executed_at) (or an EXPLAIN showing an index scan rather than 'Seq Scan on trades') would collapse H1's central mechanism.

pg_stat_statements showing the v4.5.0 trades query is low-volume or not executed on the live request path, or pg_stat_activity showing no portfolio-service sessions among the blocked/CPU-consuming set during 08:55-10:59Z, would break the causal chain from dep-5905 to the ledger-db step.
Metrics/traces showing a non-portfolio-service consumer (e.g. a batch job or a hidden writer) stepping on ledger-db in the 08:55-08:58Z bucket would redirect the origin away from dep-5905.
A positive IOPS-throttle or volume-burst-credit-exhaustion signal on ledger-db, or a distinct disk/throughput anomaly at onset, would revive H5 despite the flat disk_used_pct and replication_lag_ms.

Ledger-db log evidence of vacuum worker launch/duration or lock waits in 08:55-09:20Z would reopen H2; conversely, evidence of a shared blocking lock held by any session would point to a lock-contention mechanism rather than CPU-bound seq scans.
Rollback of dep-5905 without recovery of ledger-db cpu_pct/slow_queries/connections and order-service p99 would falsify H1 and require re-opening H3/H5.

Evidence that order-service's datasource pool ceiling is misconfigured or that it retries amplify load without request-rate growth would revive H4, though portfolio-service's simultaneous collapse and the flat app-side metrics argue against it.

order-service memory_pct and request_rate are also flat across the event: memory ~59.6-60.8% avg in all buckets 08:00-10:41Z (max 66.96), request_rate ~227-234 req/s (mean 231.22). Available metrics for order-service are cpu_pct, db_pool_in_use, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts — there is no GC or thread-pool metric to inspect.

ledger-db-side metrics available are connections_active, cpu_pct, disk_used_pct, replication_lag_ms, slow_queries_per_min (no query-latency or lock metric). ledger-db cpu_pct averages 96.11% in the 09:08 bucket and 95.69-96.16% through 10:24Z, versus a 47.34% bucket average at 08:30Z (max 96.81 already within that bucket), i.e. the DB host is CPU-pinned while the client app hosts are not.

portfolio-service latency_p99_ms — the other service that deployed against the shared ledger-db at 08:56Z — jumps in the same 08:58 bucket from ~177-183ms baseline to 6985ms avg (max 7212.58) and holds ~6.7-7.2s through 10:57Z.

payment-service latency_p99_ms stays flat ~310-326ms across the same window (min 287.66, mean 319.3) despite also holding a db edge to ledger-db, so the symptom is not uniformly hitting all ledger-db consumers.

No tool in the available surface can introspect ledger-db schema or SQL statistics: I could not run (1) a list of indexes on trades / the (account_id, executed_at) index question, (2) any EXPLAIN/query plan, (3) a trades table row count or size, or (4) a pg_stat_statements / pg_stat_activity call-count and blocked-session query for 08:00-10:59Z. Only get_config_changes, get_deployments, get_service_dependencies and search_historical_incidents were available and callable; none returns schema, plan, table-size or pg_stat data.

The only writes to ledger-db in the window remain cfg-2903 (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor 0.2 -> 0.1, 2026-05-05T08:00:00Z, dba-team) and zero ledger-db deployments — re-querying config changes with no service filter returned the same single change, and get_deployments scoped to ledger-db returned count 0. No schema change, index creation, or migration appears anywhere in the change record.

The single deployment in the whole window is still dep-5905 portfolio-service v4.5.0 at 2026-05-05T08:56:00Z, summary 'Add realised P&L breakdown to holdings API', changes ['new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at', 'no migration included'], status live, rolled_back_at null. The 'no migration included' note is the closest thing in the change record to the index question, but it is a deploy annotation, not schema evidence.

findings.statement: ledger-db disk_used_pct is flat across the entire 07:00-10:59Z window with no step at the 08:58Z onset: 10-minute buckets range 70.78-71.48% avg throughout, summary mean 71.01 (min 69.36, max 72.5), missing_points 0.

ledger-db disk_used_pct shows no change at fine 4-minute granularity around onset either: buckets span 70.56-71.81% avg from 08:30Z through 09:14Z, e.g. 08:54Z avg 71.29 and 08:58Z avg 70.69 (the onset bucket), so disk fill is not climbing into the event.

ledger-db replication_lag_ms is flat at ~40ms across 07:00-10:59Z (summary mean 40.0, min 35.43, max 43.67, missing_points 0); the 08:50Z bucket avg 40.15 and 09:00Z avg 39.52 straddle onset with no degradation.

The ledger-db metric source exposes NO IOPS, throughput, queue-depth or volume-throttle indicator: available_metrics is exactly ['connections_active','cpu_pct','disk_used_pct','replication_lag_ms','slow_queries_per_min']. IOPS-throttle behavior therefore cannot be observed directly on this DB.

settlement-service, the fourth ledger-db consumer, is completely unaffected over 07:00-10:59Z: latency_p99_ms flat at mean 240.28ms (min 209.99, max 271.99) with no onset step, error_rate flat at mean 0.22% (max 0.32), and db_pool_in_use flat at mean 6.02 connections (max 6.69).

payment-service db_pool_in_use is flat at mean 8.05 connections (min 7.27, max 9.04) across 07:00-10:59Z with no rise at onset, and payment-service emitted ZERO WARN/ERROR log entries over 08:00-10:59Z (total_matched 0 over data range 05:00-10:59Z) — consistent with a different DB access path/queries rather than a shared-saturation victim.
